name: Constraining behavior versus learning the objective
claim: Concrete Problems (2016) proposes remedies that restrict what a system can do — impact penalties, bounded exploration, formal verification — while InstructGPT and Constitutional AI (2022) instead learn the objective itself from human or AI feedback, and both families of remedy answer the same 2016 diagnosis of reward hacking and Goodhart's law.
narrative: This story follows two families of remedy across the corpus. Concrete Problems (2016) traces accidents to a mis-specified objective — reward hacking and Goodhart's law — then proposes two kinds of fix: restrict what the system can do (impact penalties, bounded exploration, formal verification, adversarial hardening), or change what it is trained to want (demonstrations, learned reward models, scalable oversight). InstructGPT (2022) and Constitutional AI (2022) build out the second family: supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and PPO in InstructGPT; critique-and-revision plus AI feedback in Constitutional AI. Both are measured against public benchmarks and against each other on a documented helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff, and both still show Goodhart-style residue — reward-model over-optimization, hedging, evasiveness. Distributional shift, the corpus's other 2016 open problem, is addressed only by the constraint family and left untouched by both 2022 papers.

children.name: The shared diagnosis: mis-specified objectives
children.narrative: Concrete Problems (2016) traces accidents — harmful unintended behavior — to a single mechanism: a system faithfully optimizing an objective that turns out to be wrong, distinct from adjacent fields such as security, fairness, and privacy, which study different causes. Its account of reward hacking lists why proxies get gamed: partial observability, complex systems, abstract rewards, feedback loops, and environments an agent can tamper with. Goodhart's law names the general pattern, and the same pattern reappears in 2022: InstructGPT's reward-model over-optimization and excessive hedging, and Constitutional AI's evasiveness, are the same failure recurring under RLHF and RL from AI feedback. The remedies that follow split along one line: restrict what the system can do, or change what it is trained to want.

Constraining what the system can do
children.narrative: Concrete Problems (2016) proposes several remedies that restrict behavior without touching the objective. Impact regularizers penalize distance from a baseline state; penalizing influence and treating other agents' interests as constraints extend the same idea. Safe exploration keeps an agent inside recoverable regions, using risk-sensitive objectives instead of expected-value optimization. Against reward hacking specifically, the paper proposes reward capping, model lookahead, trip wires, careful engineering, and adversarial-ML transplants such as adversarial reward functions and counterexample resistance. Where the stakes justify it, formal verification and control-theory tools — reachability analysis, H-infinity control — are imported to prove properties outright. None of these remedies changes what the system is optimizing for; each limits the actions or states available to it, and each requires someone to decide where the limit is placed.

Learning the objective from feedback
children.narrative: Concrete Problems (2016) also sketches remedies that work by changing the objective rather than restricting behavior: learning from demonstrations instead of a specified reward, and scalable oversight — predicting a costly-to-evaluate reward via semi-supervised reward learning, or substituting distant supervision and hierarchical decomposition when no learned predictor is available. This is the family InstructGPT (2022) and Constitutional AI (2022) develop directly. Demonstration learning becomes InstructGPT's supervised fine-tuning step. Scalable oversight becomes a documented lineage: the 2016 open problem, to InstructGPT's learned reward model trained on human preference comparisons, to Constitutional AI's feedback model, which replaces the human labeler with AI judgments guided by a written constitution. Both 2022 papers also adopt the helpful-honest-harmless framework, from Askell et al., as their shared definition of what the learned objective should be.

Building the feedback-based training pipeline
children.narrative: InstructGPT (2022) implements the objective-learning family as a three-step pipeline: supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations, a reward model trained on human preference comparisons between outputs, and PPO reinforcement learning against that reward model, held near the SFT model by a per-token KL penalty and a pretraining-data mix that limits capability regressions. This pipeline depends on human infrastructure: screened labelers, prompt collection, and inter-labeler agreement checks. Constitutional AI (2022) extends the same approach: a supervised stage of AI self-critique and revision against a written constitution produces SL-CAI, and an RL stage trains against a feedback model that applies the constitution to generate harmlessness preference labels in place of human ones — RL from AI feedback. Constitutional AI compares its results to prior dialogue agents such as LaMDA and Sparrow, whose harmlessness rules anticipate its constitution.

Measuring the learned objective's costs and benefits
children.narrative: Both 2022 papers measure their learned-objective approach against explicit benchmarks. InstructGPT reports human and preference judgments alongside automatic overlap scores (ROUGE, BLEU, F1), and checks capability loss — the alignment tax — on public NLP benchmarks, translation and summarization tasks, and dedicated truthfulness and bias benchmarks that overlap scores cannot catch. Constitutional AI uses Elo scores from crowdworker comparisons to track a documented tradeoff: increasing helpfulness training tends to reduce harmlessness and vice versa, seen in prior RLHF models, and reports that its method shifts the entire helpfulness-harmlessness frontier rather than trading along it. Both papers also document remaining failures — InstructGPT's hallucination, hedging, and reward-model over-optimization; Constitutional AI's evasiveness — which are Goodhart's law recurring inside the trained objective itself, the same pattern named in Concrete Problems (2016).

Distributional shift, left unresolved
children.narrative: Concrete Problems (2016) treats distributional shift — a system performing poorly once deployed on data unlike its training distribution — as a separate open problem from reward hacking, with its own remedies rather than an extension of either the constraint or the objective-learning family. One response relaxes the statistical assumptions tying training to test data, via covariate shift, partially specified models, and unsupervised risk estimation, so guarantees degrade rather than fail outright. The other reframes the problem conceptually, as broken software contracts or as a causal question in the tradition of Neyman, Rubin, and Pearl, with model repair as a concrete technique for restoring a violated property after the fact. Neither InstructGPT nor Constitutional AI (2022) addresses distributional shift directly; it remains a 2016 open problem outside the scope of both papers' training pipelines.

intro:
Every remedy in this corpus answers the same diagnosis, a system faithfully optimizing an objective that turns out to be wrong, but not in the same way. Some remedies restrict what the system is allowed to do; others change what it is trained to want instead.

The chapters move from that shared diagnosis, through Concrete Problems' constraint-based remedies and its learning-based seeds, into the pipeline InstructGPT and Constitutional AI actually built and what it cost and gained, closing on distributional shift, the one problem neither family resolves. Open one chapter at a time; the controls above the tree set how much detail you see.
